concept.name: Inventory risk
concept.definition: The price risk a market maker bears on positions accumulated while quoting both sides of the market, because bids and offers are hit asymmetrically before price moves. In the Ho-Stoll lineage formalized by Avellaneda-Stoikov and solved under inventory constraints by Gueant, Lehalle and Fernandez-Tapia (2013), the market maker's P&L from the spread is challenged by the price risk borne on inventory.
concept.intuition: Earning the spread means repeatedly holding stock you did not choose to hold; if the price moves while you hold it, the spread income can be overwhelmed.
concept.mechanics: Buy and sell orders arrive at rates that depend on quote placement, so inventory wanders from target; optimal quotes shift downward when long and upward when short to attract offsetting flow, with the skew increasing in volatility, risk aversion, and remaining horizon.
concept.failure_modes: In one-way markets inventory control breaks down and providers widen or withdraw entirely, amplifying liquidity crises; capital and margin constraints further limit inventory absorption in stress.
concept.misconceptions: Market makers are not automatically direction-neutral - neutrality is actively and imperfectly managed, and residual inventory exposure is a core cost of liquidity provision.
concept.example: A market maker accumulates a 10,000-share long position in a falling market and shades both quotes two cents lower to attract buyers and slow further accumulation.

citations.source: Gueant, Lehalle and Fernandez-Tapia, 'Dealing with the Inventory Risk: A Solution to the Market Making Problem', Mathematics and Financial Economics 7(4):477-507 (arXiv preprint)
